items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6272: Wearable Sensor Fusion for Psychophysiological Arousal Recognition in Air Traffic Control: A Fuzzy MCDM Approach
items.summary: Recognizing psychophysiological arousal and strain from wearable sensors extends affective computing beyond discrete-emotion classification. Vigilance decrement during air traffic control (ATC) shifts illustrates this: the psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) cannot be administered while a controller is working. We develop and evaluate a wearable, label-free Vigilance/Strain Risk Index (F-VRI) for ATC operators, fusing five physiological signals via entropy-weighted fuzzy TOPSIS. The index was assessed in two samples: 38 controllers measured pre/post shift (preliminary, pilot-level evidence) and 13 trainees pre/post across simulator sessions (confirmatory validation). Compared with PVT, the fused index detected the pre/post change more reliably at the group level (simulator: p = 0.004 vs. p = 0.379) and at the individual level (68-80% directional concordance vs. 33-55% for PVT, at or below chance). Compared with five supervised machine learning baselines, the fuzzy index was the only method to remain significant under cross-domain transfer (both p < 0.05), while every supervised model failed in at least one direction. An exploratory extension revealed a weighting pathology in which static covariates absorbed disproportionate model weight, which led us to a two-layer state/trait architecture. These results support fuzzy MCDM as an interpretable sensor-fusion framework for psychophysiological state monitoring under uncertainty, with continuous, streaming deployment remaining a prospective extension requiring further validation; the field-cohort effect (p = 0.084) remains at the pilot level.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6277: A Comprehensive Review on Self-Powered Wearable Photonic Sensors: Materials, Photophysics, and System Integration
items.summary: Self-powered wearable photonic sensors enable energy-autonomous operation by integrating optical sensing, energy harvesting, and signal transduction within a unified platform. These systems exploit photophysical mechanisms such as photovoltaic, photogating, and triboelectric effects to convert ambient or body-derived energy into electrical signals while simultaneously performing sensing. Advances in hybrid semiconductors, two-dimensional materials, and nanocomposites have significantly improved light absorption, carrier transport, and mechanical compliance, enabling integration into flexible and textile-based wearable formats. Device architectures have evolved from simple junctions to heterostructured and tandem configurations that enhance spectral selectivity and energy utilization under variable illumination. However, reliable operation under low-intensity and dynamically changing conditions remains a key challenge, particularly in balancing sensing performance with energy autonomy. This review analyzes the interplay between materials, photophysical mechanisms, device architectures, and system-level design, with emphasis on energy harvesting-sensing co-optimization. Challenges related to mechanical stability, signal reliability, and real-world deployment are discussed, alongside emerging solutions based on adaptive photonic systems and intelligent data processing. These insights provide a framework for next-generation wearable photonic platforms for healthcare, environmental monitoring, and human-machine interfaces.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6259: MDT-HMTL: A Multidimensional Temporal Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning Framework for Myocardial Infarction Detection and State Classification Using PPG Signals
items.summary: Continuous assessment of myocardial infarction (MI) using photoplethysmography (PPG) signals has potential for out-of-hospital cardiovascular monitoring, yet conventional single-channel and short-window approaches have limitations in capturing complex hemodynamic variations and dynamic disease-state transitions. To address these limitations, we propose MDT-HMTL, a Multidimensional Temporal Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning framework tailored for simultaneous MI detection and disease-state classification. By integrating multi-channel physiological representations with hierarchical temporal modeling, MDT-HMTL captures local morphological characteristics and longer-range temporal dependencies within a unified multi-task architecture. Evaluation on the MIMIC-III clinical database achieved an average area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.908 and an overall accuracy of 86.4%. Furthermore, ablation studies demonstrated the contributions of multi-dimensional representation learning and hierarchical temporal modeling to the overall performance. The proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of PPG-based MI detection and longitudinal disease-state assessment, highlighting its potential for future non-invasive and wearable-compatible cardiovascular monitoring.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6267: An Adaptive State- and Morphology-Based Four-Event Segmentation Algorithm for Sit-to-Stand-to-Sit Cycles from Wii Balance Board Load Signals: An Exploratory Comparison with Noraxon Report-Consistent IMU Timing
items.summary: Sit-to-stand (STS) tests are often summarized by completion time or repetition count; however, phase-specific analysis requires reproducible operational segmentation. We developed an adaptive state- and morphology-based algorithm that identified ten internal anchors in Wii Balance Board (WBB) vertical-load waveforms and derived an ordered P1-P4 chain representing cycle start, end of sit-to-stand, start of stand-to-sit, and cycle end, respectively. The algorithm was developed using 108 T1-T3 trials and then applied unchanged to a temporally separate batch of 24 T0 trials. Fourteen T0 participants overlapped with development and 10 were included in a descriptive subset of participants not represented in the development dataset. Complete chains were identified in 24/24 T0 trials and 10/10 descriptive-subset trials (100%; exact 95% CI, 69.2%-100%), versus 7/24 for the prespecified internal non-adaptive baseline. Complete-chain identification remained 100% across all three datasets under one-at-a-time perturbations of +/-10% and +/-20% of 52 frozen numerical parameters, although selected sit-down rules shifted local boundaries. Removing the separate seated-baseline/fallback component reduced complete-chain identification to 101/108, 12/24, and 8/10. Across 131 paired trials, WBB total-cycle duration differed from Noraxon software (MR 4.2.34 Software; Noraxon, Scottsdale, AZ, USA)-reported duration by -0.188 s (95% CI, -0.313 to -0.060). These differences reflect distinct operational timing definitions rather than error against an independent reference standard. Independent reference-event and external clinical studies remain necessary.

items.title: Noninvasive Interstitial Glucose Estimation Using Wearables and Machine Learning in Healthy Individuals and Individuals With Obesity: Observational Cohort Study
items.summary: Background: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) can facilitate weight management and lower the risk of metabolic diseases by providing real-time feedback on glycemic responses, thereby enabling more informed lifestyle decisions. However, current CGM systems remain constrained by invasiveness, cost, and short sensor lifespan, limiting their practicality for guiding individualized postprandial low-glycemic diets. Objective: Extending earlier proof-of-concept findings, this study aimed to validate an interstitial glucose (IG) machine learning algorithm in real-world environments using multimodal, continuous data collected from wearable sensors and smartwatches. In the long term, we aim to embed a noninvasive, sensor-based algorithm for estimating tissue glucose within mobile health apps and postprandial low-glycemic diet frameworks to enable scalable, personalized prevention strategies. Methods: We conducted a 2-week study phase during which participants continuously wore 2 noninvasive sensor devices: a scientific sensor wristband (Empatica EmbracePlus) and a commercially available smartwatch (Fitbit Sense 2). As a reference measurement, an invasive CGM sensor (Abbott FreeStyle Libre 3) measured IG levels. For metabolic characterization, 1-point fasting blood and urine samples were collected, and deep phenotyping using state-of-the-art nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and bioelectrical impedance analysis was performed. For participants with overweight and obesity, clinical standard parameters focusing on glucose metabolism were analyzed. Results: A total of 74 participants, 34 (46%) healthy controls and 40 (54%) metabolically at-risk (MR) individuals, simultaneously used an invasive CGM device together with 2 noninvasive wristbands over 2 weeks. Healthy controls were characterized by a mean age of 24.53 (SD 3.68) years and a mean BMI of 22.36 (SD 2.16) kg/m². In contrast, the MR cohort had a mean age of 55.38 (SD 15.08) years and a mean BMI of 35.38 (SD 4.91) kg

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6230: ECG Vertex-Time Activation Representation for IoT-XR Heart Monitoring
items.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring via wearable devices generates rich physiological data, yet conventional time-domain representations offer limited support for spatial interpretation and immersive visualization. We introduce a novel vertex-time representation of the ECG signal, introducing the Ideal Vertex Time (IVT) and Eigen Vertex Time (EVT) vectors which map temporal activation intervals and eigenbeat amplitudes onto a three-dimensional heart point cloud. A key novelty is that this approach serves a dual purpose: it enables graph-spectral ECG feature extraction for classification tasks, and it drives immersive rendering within an Internet of Things pipeline, based on MQTT, cloud processing, and Extended Reality visualization. This work is presented as a proof of concept. The mapping from ECG landmarks to anatomical regions is model-driven and has not been independently validated against patient-specific electrophysiological measurements. Herein, the framework is evaluated for classification purposes on an affective-state dataset and integrated into an Internet-of-Things-enabled e-health monitoring pipeline, whose prototype replays previously recorded ECG signals rather than acquiring them from a wearable device. Overall, this work extends conventional time-domain electrocardiographic analysis toward a spatially structured and immersive monitoring framework. No comparison with conventional ECG descriptors was performed; thus, no advantage over such features is claimed. Its clinical utility remains to be assessed within a patient-specific monitoring pipeline, computing the vertex-time features alongside conventional ECG descriptors and weighting them jointly to identify the best representation for each patient.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6202: Driving-Context Classification from Wearable Physiological and Motion Signals During Real-World Driving
items.summary: Wearable physiological sensing is widely used in driving research to infer drowsiness and stress, but whether driving context itself is reflected in wearable signals, independent of any drowsiness label, is rarely examined directly; any such signal reflects the driver's physiological response to context, not the road environment itself. We analyzed 1536 non-overlapping 60-s windows from 18 driving sessions completed by 11 drivers wearing an Empatica EmbracePlus across three fixed real-world routes (Rural, Highway, Urban; round-trip distances 22.4-47.1 km). items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6235: Temporal Step Supervision for Robust Step Counting from Wearable Accelerometers
items.summary: Step-counting remains difficult in irregular walking, where step timing and signal patterns are less consistent than in controlled walking. We propose a step-counting model that uses step timing annotations as temporal supervision during training. Each step timestamp is expanded into a short temporal label interval, and a U-Net is used to localize step events because its dense prediction structure is well suited to temporal localization. The model is trained to estimate both where steps occur in the window and how many steps the window contains. The final count is obtained by summing the predicted values over time and dividing by the label width. On the Clemson wrist-worn dataset, the model achieves MAPE values of 4.61%, 9.90%, and 15.78% under regular, semi-regular, and irregular walking, respectively. Compared with classical step-detection algorithms and reproduced CNN, WaveNet, and LSTM baselines, the proposed model shows substantially lower error under irregular walking. On OxWalk, the model achieves 13.06% MAPE using only OxWalk training data, reaching performance comparable to fine-tuned Stepcount SSL, which relies on large-scale self-supervised pretraining. These results suggest that temporal step supervision improves robustness under irregular walking and can reduce dependence on large-scale external pretraining.

Methods: We conducted a model-based economic evaluation comparing CVRM-Box with care as usual in Dutch primary care integrated CVRM programs. items.title: Patient-level evaluation of smartwatch-based pain and dehydration detection in nursing home residents: a prospective observational study
items.summary: IntroductionNursing home residents are at high risk for underrecognized pain and dehydration, particularly those with cognitive impairment who cannot reliably self-report symptoms. Consumer-grade smartwatches capable of continuous physiological monitoring may help detect these conditions, but their feasibility in frail older adults remains underexplored, and evaluation strategies based on random splits of repeated time windows can yield optimistically biased estimates. We therefore evaluated the feasibility of continuous smartwatch monitoring in nursing home residents and explored whether machine learning models using smartwatch-derived data can detect pain and dehydration under patient-independent evaluation.MethodsIn a prospective, observational feasibility study (VIENNESE) conducted at three Caritas nursing homes in Vienna, Austria (February to November 2024), 24 residents were enrolled, 16 began smartwatch monitoring and 13 completed the protocol and contributed sufficient data for analysis (1,414 labelled 120 min windows). Matched XGBoost classifiers were evaluated with nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation, with hyperparameters tuned inside each fold on training participants only.ResultsPain detection showed a weak signal, with a mean per-patient AUC of 0.557 (range 0.533 to 0.599 across random seeds) and a pooled window-level AUC of 0.736 (0.662 to 0.784). For dehydration, discrimination remained at chance level (mean per-patient AUC 0.513, range 0.468 to 0.550; pooled 0.484, range 0.393 to 0.593).DiscussionContinuous smartwatch monitoring was operationally feasible in this population. The exploratory models point to a weak pain-related signal that merits evaluation in larger cohorts with stronger reference standards, whereas hydration status may require different sensing modalities.

items.summary: Background: The timed up-and-go (TUG) test is a mobility-related functional task commonly performed in clinical practice for a variety of clinical applications. items.title: Mental health monitoring in the workplace using artificial intelligence: A scoping review
items.summary: by Kalee Jack, Julie Tian, Viktoriia Kurkova, Setayesh Modanloo, Liz Dennett, Jasmine Noble, Andrew Greenshaw, Jake Hayward Workplace mental health issues are a prevalent concern. A potential solution is remote health monitoring. In this scoping review, we map evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) for workplace mental health monitoring. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science were searched until March 2024. Studies that evaluated AI for monitoring of a common workplace mental health concern in an actual workplace setting were included. Thirteen studies were included; most (8/13, 62%) were conducted in an office environment, and 4/13 (31%) were in healthcare. Most studies monitored stress (10/13, 77%). The most common method was wearable sensors (8/13, 62%). Studies monitored a wide variety of parameters; the most common were physical activity (7/13, 54%), heart rate or heart rate variability (7/13, 54%). A wide variety of participant-report surveys, including validated (7/13, 54%) and non-validated (6/13, 46%) surveys, were used to measure mental health outcomes. Studies employed diverse AI methods, including supervised, semi-supervised and other (Markov chain and Monte Carlo). The most common AI models used were support vector machines (5/13, 38%), decision trees (5/13, 38%), naive Bayes (4/13, 31%), and random forest (4/13, 38%). Model accuracy ranged from 62%-99%. Future work should identify standard metrics to enable cross-comparability and use larger, high-quality datasets for enriched training, advanced optimization techniques, and careful model tuning.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6272: Wearable Sensor Fusion for Psychophysiological Arousal Recognition in Air Traffic Control: A Fuzzy MCDM Approach
academic.summary: Recognizing psychophysiological arousal and strain from wearable sensors extends affective computing beyond discrete-emotion classification. Vigilance decrement during air traffic control (ATC) shifts illustrates this: the psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) cannot be administered while a controller is working. We develop and evaluate a wearable, label-free Vigilance/Strain Risk Index (F-VRI) for ATC operators, fusing five physiological signals via entropy-weighted fuzzy TOPSIS. The index was assessed in two samples: 38 controllers measured pre/post shift (preliminary, pilot-level evidence) and 13 trainees pre/post across simulator sessions (confirmatory validation). Compared with PVT, the fused index detected the pre/post change more reliably at the group level (simulator: p = 0.004 vs. p = 0.379) and at the individual level (68-80% directional concordance vs. 33-55% for PVT, at or below chance). Compared with five supervised machine learning baselines, the fuzzy index was the only method to remain significant under cross-domain transfer (both p < 0.05), while every supervised model failed in at least one direction. An exploratory extension revealed a weighting pathology in which static covariates absorbed disproportionate model weight, which led us to a two-layer state/trait architecture. These results support fuzzy MCDM as an interpretable sensor-fusion framework for psychophysiological state monitoring under uncertainty, with continuous, streaming deployment remaining a prospective extension requiring further validation; the field-cohort effect (p = 0.084) remains at the pilot level.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6277: A Comprehensive Review on Self-Powered Wearable Photonic Sensors: Materials, Photophysics, and System Integration
academic.summary: Self-powered wearable photonic sensors enable energy-autonomous operation by integrating optical sensing, energy harvesting, and signal transduction within a unified platform. These systems exploit photophysical mechanisms such as photovoltaic, photogating, and triboelectric effects to convert ambient or body-derived energy into electrical signals while simultaneously performing sensing. Advances in hybrid semiconductors, two-dimensional materials, and nanocomposites have significantly improved light absorption, carrier transport, and mechanical compliance, enabling integration into flexible and textile-based wearable formats. Device architectures have evolved from simple junctions to heterostructured and tandem configurations that enhance spectral selectivity and energy utilization under variable illumination. However, reliable operation under low-intensity and dynamically changing conditions remains a key challenge, particularly in balancing sensing performance with energy autonomy. This review analyzes the interplay between materials, photophysical mechanisms, device architectures, and system-level design, with emphasis on energy harvesting-sensing co-optimization. Challenges related to mechanical stability, signal reliability, and real-world deployment are discussed, alongside emerging solutions based on adaptive photonic systems and intelligent data processing. These insights provide a framework for next-generation wearable photonic platforms for healthcare, environmental monitoring, and human-machine interfaces.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6259: MDT-HMTL: A Multidimensional Temporal Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning Framework for Myocardial Infarction Detection and State Classification Using PPG Signals
academic.summary: Continuous assessment of myocardial infarction (MI) using photoplethysmography (PPG) signals has potential for out-of-hospital cardiovascular monitoring, yet conventional single-channel and short-window approaches have limitations in capturing complex hemodynamic variations and dynamic disease-state transitions. To address these limitations, we propose MDT-HMTL, a Multidimensional Temporal Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning framework tailored for simultaneous MI detection and disease-state classification. By integrating multi-channel physiological representations with hierarchical temporal modeling, MDT-HMTL captures local morphological characteristics and longer-range temporal dependencies within a unified multi-task architecture. Evaluation on the MIMIC-III clinical database achieved an average area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.908 and an overall accuracy of 86.4%. Furthermore, ablation studies demonstrated the contributions of multi-dimensional representation learning and hierarchical temporal modeling to the overall performance. The proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of PPG-based MI detection and longitudinal disease-state assessment, highlighting its potential for future non-invasive and wearable-compatible cardiovascular monitoring.

Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6267: An Adaptive State- and Morphology-Based Four-Event Segmentation Algorithm for Sit-to-Stand-to-Sit Cycles from Wii Balance Board Load Signals: An Exploratory Comparison with Noraxon Report-Consistent IMU Timing
academic.summary: Sit-to-stand (STS) tests are often summarized by completion time or repetition count; however, phase-specific analysis requires reproducible operational segmentation. We developed an adaptive state- and morphology-based algorithm that identified ten internal anchors in Wii Balance Board (WBB) vertical-load waveforms and derived an ordered P1-P4 chain representing cycle start, end of sit-to-stand, start of stand-to-sit, and cycle end, respectively. The algorithm was developed using 108 T1-T3 trials and then applied unchanged to a temporally separate batch of 24 T0 trials. Fourteen T0 participants overlapped with development and 10 were included in a descriptive subset of participants not represented in the development dataset. Complete chains were identified in 24/24 T0 trials and 10/10 descriptive-subset trials (100%; exact 95% CI, 69.2%-100%), versus 7/24 for the prespecified internal non-adaptive baseline. Complete-chain identification remained 100% across all three datasets under one-at-a-time perturbations of +/-10% and +/-20% of 52 frozen numerical parameters, although selected sit-down rules shifted local boundaries. Removing the separate seated-baseline/fallback component reduced complete-chain identification to 101/108, 12/24, and 8/10. Across 131 paired trials, WBB total-cycle duration differed from Noraxon software (MR 4.2.34 Software; Noraxon, Scottsdale, AZ, USA)-reported duration by -0.188 s (95% CI, -0.313 to -0.060). These differences reflect distinct operational timing definitions rather than error against an independent reference standard. Independent reference-event and external clinical studies remain necessary.

academic.summary: Background: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) can facilitate weight management and lower the risk of metabolic diseases by providing real-time feedback on glycemic responses, thereby enabling more informed lifestyle decisions. However, current CGM systems remain constrained by invasiveness, cost, and short sensor lifespan, limiting their practicality for guiding individualized postprandial low-glycemic diets. For metabolic characterization, 1-point fasting blood and urine samples were collected, and deep phenotyping using state-of-the-art nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and bioelectrical impedance analysis was performed. academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6230: ECG Vertex-Time Activation Representation for IoT-XR Heart Monitoring
academic.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring via wearable devices generates rich physiological data, yet conventional time-domain representations offer limited support for spatial interpretation and immersive visualization. We introduce a novel vertex-time representation of the ECG signal, introducing the Ideal Vertex Time (IVT) and Eigen Vertex Time (EVT) vectors which map temporal activation intervals and eigenbeat amplitudes onto a three-dimensional heart point cloud. A key novelty is that this approach serves a dual purpose: it enables graph-spectral ECG feature extraction for classification tasks, and it drives immersive rendering within an Internet of Things pipeline, based on MQTT, cloud processing, and Extended Reality visualization. This work is presented as a proof of concept. The mapping from ECG landmarks to anatomical regions is model-driven and has not been independently validated against patient-specific electrophysiological measurements. Herein, the framework is evaluated for classification purposes on an affective-state dataset and integrated into an Internet-of-Things-enabled e-health monitoring pipeline, whose prototype replays previously recorded ECG signals rather than acquiring them from a wearable device. Overall, this work extends conventional time-domain electrocardiographic analysis toward a spatially structured and immersive monitoring framework. No comparison with conventional ECG descriptors was performed; thus, no advantage over such features is claimed. Its clinical utility remains to be assessed within a patient-specific monitoring pipeline, computing the vertex-time features alongside conventional ECG descriptors and weighting them jointly to identify the best representation for each patient.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6235: Temporal Step Supervision for Robust Step Counting from Wearable Accelerometers
academic.summary: Step-counting remains difficult in irregular walking, where step timing and signal patterns are less consistent than in controlled walking. We propose a step-counting model that uses step timing annotations as temporal supervision during training. Each step timestamp is expanded into a short temporal label interval, and a U-Net is used to localize step events because its dense prediction structure is well suited to temporal localization. The model is trained to estimate both where steps occur in the window and how many steps the window contains. The final count is obtained by summing the predicted values over time and dividing by the label width. On the Clemson wrist-worn dataset, the model achieves MAPE values of 4.61%, 9.90%, and 15.78% under regular, semi-regular, and irregular walking, respectively. Compared with classical step-detection algorithms and reproduced CNN, WaveNet, and LSTM baselines, the proposed model shows substantially lower error under irregular walking. On OxWalk, the model achieves 13.06% MAPE using only OxWalk training data, reaching performance comparable to fine-tuned Stepcount SSL, which relies on large-scale self-supervised pretraining. These results suggest that temporal step supervision improves robustness under irregular walking and can reduce dependence on large-scale external pretraining.

academic.summary: Background: Remote patient management (RPM) that supports patient self-monitoring of vital parameters and lifestyle factors may improve cardiovascular risk management (CVRM) in primary care. However, large-scale implementation remains limited, partly due to insufficient evidence on long-term value for money, budget impact, and implications for health care professionals' workload. A time-inhomogeneous cohort Markov model simulated lifetime transitions among health states, including at-risk, post–myocardial infarction (MI), poststroke, recurrent events, cardiovascular death, and noncardiovascular death. Cardiovascular risks were modeled using prediction equations (SCORE2, SCORE2-OP, and SMART2) populated with subgroup-specific risk factor profiles. academic.title: Patient-level evaluation of smartwatch-based pain and dehydration detection in nursing home residents: a prospective observational study
academic.summary: IntroductionNursing home residents are at high risk for underrecognized pain and dehydration, particularly those with cognitive impairment who cannot reliably self-report symptoms. Consumer-grade smartwatches capable of continuous physiological monitoring may help detect these conditions, but their feasibility in frail older adults remains underexplored, and evaluation strategies based on random splits of repeated time windows can yield optimistically biased estimates. We therefore evaluated the feasibility of continuous smartwatch monitoring in nursing home residents and explored whether machine learning models using smartwatch-derived data can detect pain and dehydration under patient-independent evaluation.MethodsIn a prospective, observational feasibility study (VIENNESE) conducted at three Caritas nursing homes in Vienna, Austria (February to November 2024), 24 residents were enrolled, 16 began smartwatch monitoring and 13 completed the protocol and contributed sufficient data for analysis (1,414 labelled 120 min windows). Matched XGBoost classifiers were evaluated with nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation, with hyperparameters tuned inside each fold on training participants only.ResultsPain detection showed a weak signal, with a mean per-patient AUC of 0.557 (range 0.533 to 0.599 across random seeds) and a pooled window-level AUC of 0.736 (0.662 to 0.784). For dehydration, discrimination remained at chance level (mean per-patient AUC 0.513, range 0.468 to 0.550; pooled 0.484, range 0.393 to 0.593).DiscussionContinuous smartwatch monitoring was operationally feasible in this population. The exploratory models point to a weak pain-related signal that merits evaluation in larger cohorts with stronger reference standards, whereas hydration status may require different sensing modalities.

academic.title: Mental health monitoring in the workplace using artificial intelligence: A scoping review
academic.summary: by Kalee Jack, Julie Tian, Viktoriia Kurkova, Setayesh Modanloo, Liz Dennett, Jasmine Noble, Andrew Greenshaw, Jake Hayward Workplace mental health issues are a prevalent concern. A potential solution is remote health monitoring. In this scoping review, we map evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) for workplace mental health monitoring. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science were searched until March 2024. Studies that evaluated AI for monitoring of a common workplace mental health concern in an actual workplace setting were included. Thirteen studies were included; most (8/13, 62%) were conducted in an office environment, and 4/13 (31%) were in healthcare. Most studies monitored stress (10/13, 77%). The most common method was wearable sensors (8/13, 62%). Studies monitored a wide variety of parameters; the most common were physical activity (7/13, 54%), heart rate or heart rate variability (7/13, 54%). A wide variety of participant-report surveys, including validated (7/13, 54%) and non-validated (6/13, 46%) surveys, were used to measure mental health outcomes. Studies employed diverse AI methods, including supervised, semi-supervised and other (Markov chain and Monte Carlo). The most common AI models used were support vector machines (5/13, 38%), decision trees (5/13, 38%), naive Bayes (4/13, 31%), and random forest (4/13, 38%). Model accuracy ranged from 62%-99%. Future work should identify standard metrics to enable cross-comparability and use larger, high-quality datasets for enriched training, advanced optimization techniques, and careful model tuning.

clinical_regulatory.title: Development of a Wearable Point of Care Monitoring Device for Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea
clinical_regulatory.summary: Status: RECRUITING | Conditions: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea | Primary outcomes: ScO2, StO2: peripheral tissue oxygen saturation (StO2), traditional polysomnography measures (SpO2, respiratory effort) | Summary: Background: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) occurs when the blockage of the airway causes a person to stop breathing involuntarily for 10 seconds or more throughout the night during sleep. Pediatric OSA can be especially concerning and can have long-term effects. Researchers want to see how a monitoring device called near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) compares with the traditional techniques used in children s sleep studies. Objective: To learn about oxygen levels in the brain and limbs in children with and without sleep apnea using a wearable, point-of-care biosensor. Eligibility: Children aged 3-12 who have OSA and plan to receive treatment (OSA group) or who do not have OSA (NORM group). Design: Participants will be screened with a review of their medical records. If they have taken part in other NIH studies, that data will be reviewed as well. Participants in the NORM group will have 1 overnight study visit. Those in the OSA group will have 2 overnight study visits. Participants will do an overnight sleep study. They will have a physical exam and medical history. They will have a sleep study electroencephalography (EEG). For this, electrodes will be placed on their head. They will wear a gauze cap to keep the electrodes in place. Two NIRS probes made of a soft silicon will be placed on their forehead and arm. They will follow their normal bedtime routine. Their parent will stay overnight. The OSA group will have a second study visit 2 weeks to 12 months after they start treatment for their sleep apnea. They will repeat the sleep study.

scarcityTaxonomy.note: Top Signals selection rubric. Each Top Signals item MUST be labeled with exactly one category from `categories`, assigned a frequency anchor (`annual`/`quarterly`/`monthly`), and scored as `base_score × anchor_weight`. LLM only does category+anchor matching — it does NOT need historical knowledge (categories define scarcity, not LLM memory). Revise quarterly based on dogfooding.

anchor_definitions.annual: Once-a-year or rarer event within this category (e.g., FDA's first consumer-grade AFib clearance for a wearable — happens at most once a year globally).
anchor_definitions.quarterly: Few-per-year event within this category (e.g., a major vendor's new regulatory clearance in a new jurisdiction).
anchor_definitions.monthly: Routine-but-still-notable within this category (e.g., another vendor achieving a similar clearance that's already established).

categories.criteria: FDA 510(k) / De Novo / PMA, CE mark MDR, NMPA certification, PMDA, TGA — for a wearable health feature. Peer-reviewed multi-site prospective clinical validation also qualifies.
examples_positive: Apple Watch gets FDA clearance for new sleep apnea detection
Samsung Health Monitor BP approved in US
Oura ring NMPA class-II certification
examples_negative: Another vendor clones an already-approved feature in a new region (→ monthly anchor, not annual)

categories.criteria: Company or academic publicly releases model weights, pretrained foundation model, large labeled dataset, or production-grade SDK/code for wearable/physiological signals. Must be usable (not just a paper claiming 'code coming soon').
examples_positive: Meta releases wearable foundation model weights on HuggingFace
Stanford/Apple release 1M-ECG labeled dataset
Google open-sources Fitbit sleep staging model
examples_negative: Academic paper promises code release but repo is empty

categories.criteria: M&A, major exec/founder departure or appointment at a wearable company, large funding round (≥$50M), strategic pivot announcement. Affects competitive landscape or talent flow.
examples_positive: Google acquires Oura
Shwetak Patel leaves Google Health for X startup
WHOOP pivots from consumer to B2B-clinical

categories.criteria: Consumer wearable first-time integration of a physical/biochemical sensing modality (non-invasive BP, non-invasive glucose, EMG, sweat cortisol, SpHb, real-time hydration, etc.). Must ship in a real product, not just a research paper.
examples_positive: Samsung ships first consumer non-invasive glucose on Galaxy Watch
Apple adds wrist-based cuffless BP to Series X
Oura integrates continuous sweat-lactate sensor
examples_negative: New optical HR sensor iteration in existing form factor (already-done modality)
Academic prototype for a new sensor — belongs in algorithmic_breakthrough or open_release if qualifying

categories.criteria: New SOTA with concrete metric on wearable/physiological task, OR foundation-model / self-supervised training at ≥10M-sample scale, OR on-device breakthrough with specific latency/size/power numbers. Must have reproducible evidence (paper with code, benchmark result).
examples_positive: ECG foundation model at 11M samples with systematic SSL comparison (example)
On-device AFib detection at <5ms/inference on Apple S10 chip
New sleep-stage SOTA on SHHS with 3pp gain
examples_negative: Incremental +1pp gain with cherry-picked test set

categories.criteria: Prospective or multi-site clinical study with n≥10,000 participants OR multi-center design, wearable-derived endpoint, peer-reviewed or at top conference.
examples_positive: Ultrahuman Ring N=3086 longitudinal sleep study (today's example — note: n<10k but near-threshold + longitudinal design keeps it in this category at monthly anchor)
All of Us cohort wearable analysis n>50k
Apple Heart Study n=419k

categories.criteria: Wearable vendor first-time entry into new go-to-market category: clinical services, B2B/B2B2C, insurance, subscription, EHR integration, pharma partnership. Must be a real product launch, not a trial balloon.
examples_positive: WHOOP launches clinician video visits + HealthEx EHR integration (today's example)
Oura partners with large insurer for reimbursed rings
Apple Watch Atrial Fibrillation History gets CMS reimbursement code
examples_negative: New subscription tier of existing product
